title: Maryland’s other death tax is a punishment for not having children
summary: Maryland's inheritance tax is subtle discriminator, writes Steven Messmer: Most people can avoid paying the 10% tax on inheritances by leaving it to a spouse, child, grandchild or sibling, but that's not an option for those with no children or family.
content:
by Steven Messmer, Maryland Matters January 22, 2026

by Steven Messmer, Maryland Matters January 22, 2026

When people talk about the “death tax,” they mean the estate tax, a tax on the ultra-wealthy. But Maryland has another death tax — the Maryland inheritance tax, a tax on non-wealthy Marylanders who did not have children.

The Maryland inheritance tax is often conflated with the estate taxes, so people assume that this is a tax on the wealthy. In fact, it’s a tax that only burdens non-wealthy people. More precisely, wealthy people do pay the inheritance tax, but it counts as a credit against the Maryland estate tax, so the inheritance tax does not cost them anything. This bizarre result is due to history, not intentional policy. You can also avoid the tax if you have a second home in another state or a trust.

The Maryland inheritance tax is very subtle in how it discriminates. It is a 10% tax on inheritances. But most people don’t need to pay it because an inheritance left to a spouse, child, grandchild or sibling is exempt.

If we rephrase that slightly, it’s a tax on leaving an inheritance beyond your nuclear family and lineal descendants. For those that did not have children, they have no options to leave an inheritance to someone of a younger generation without being taxed. And for those that did not get married, they will likely be taxed when leaving an inheritance to their partner. In effect, it’s a punishment on those that did not form a “traditional nuclear family.”

It’s a tax on leaving an inheritance to nieces, nephews, cousins, friends and unmarried romantic partners, no matter how close the relationship is. The familial exemptions are not an objective assessment of which relationships are worthy of protection, they are only a list of who the legislature has decided to count as family. Maryland law prohibits discrimination based on marital and familial status in employment and housing, but not in death.

LGBTQ+ people are particularly vulnerable to the tax as they’re about half as likely to be married and substantially less likely to be parents. When they pass their assets to their loved ones, they are taxed while most others are not.

The Maryland inheritance tax was adopted before the Civil War. In 1848, Maryland’s highest court ruled that enslaved people freed through a will had to pay inheritance tax on their freedom.

In the 20th century, almost every state had an inheritance tax and every state had a state estate tax. Now, only five states still have an inheritance tax, and only 12 have an estate tax. Maryland is the only state left with both.

The tax is riddled with arbitrary distinctions. Leave an inheritance to a brother or half-brother – no tax. Leave an inheritance to a stepbrother or brother-in-law – it’s taxed. Name a beneficiary on a life insurance policy – no tax. Forget to do so – taxed. Cash in another state – no tax. A bank account in another state – taxed.

The inheritance tax only raises about $75 million per year statewide—enough to cover 0.15% of Maryland’s operating budget. Just to show how little this is, if we raised the sales tax from 6% to 6.08%, it would cover the cost of repealing the inheritance tax. Like increasing the sales tax by eight cents on the sale of a $100 pair of shoes.

The stumbling block to repealing the inheritance tax is that the registers of wills use the inheritance tax as their dedicated funding source. In 2000, the inheritance tax was repealed for descendants, spouses and siblings. To repeal it entirely, the proposal was to increase probate fees to fund the registers, which failed. In 2025, the governor’s office tried to repeal the inheritance tax. The proposal was to increase the Maryland estate tax to fund the registers, but it also failed.

I propose that the registers be funded like most other state agencies— through an appropriation in the budget. If you’re trying to advance justice, but you’re unwilling to pay for it or offend anyone, you’re trying to make an omelet without cracking an egg.

The inheritance tax is Maryland’s fiscal appendix. We feel the pain from the inflammation of injustice, but we are afraid to undergo the needed surgery. So, we treat its symptoms, creating one more exemption or one more rule, each time adding administrative burden and reducing fiscal relevance. It is time to cut out the appendix. It will hurt for the moment, but we will heal back stronger than before.
